content: Approximately half of individuals diagnosed with myasthenia gravis initially exhibit symptoms confined to the eyes, a condition referred to as ocular myasthenia. Among these patients, 50% to 60% progress to generalized myasthenia gravis, with most cases transitioning within two years of onset. The optimal management of ocular myasthenia remains a subject of debate. This review represents an update of prior analyses published in 2006, 2008, and 2010. The primary objectives of this review were to evaluate the effectiveness of treatments for ocular myasthenia and to address three specific questions: (1) Are there any treatments that reduce the likelihood of progression from ocular myasthenia to generalized myasthenia gravis? (2) Are there any treatments that alleviate symptoms such as double vision (diplopia) or drooping eyelids (ptosis)? (3) What is the incidence of adverse effects associated with the treatments used for ocular myasthenia? For this updated review, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Neuromuscular Disease Group Specialized Register (as of August 3, 2012), CENTRAL (Issue 7, 2012), MEDLINE (from January 1996 to July 2012), and EMBASE (from January 1974 to July 2012). The search focused on identifying randomized controlled trials (RCTs), as well as case-control and cohort studies. Both authors independently reviewed the titles and abstracts of all identified articles, and full texts of potentially relevant studies were examined. References from included manuscripts were also reviewed to identify additional relevant studies, and experts in the field were consulted to uncover any unpublished or additional data. When necessary, study authors were contacted for further clarification or information. To be included in the review, studies had to meet three criteria: (a) they had to employ a randomized or quasi-randomized controlled study design; (b) they had to compare an active treatment to a placebo, no treatment, or another treatment; and (c) they had to report results specifically for patients with ocular myasthenia (classified as grade 1 according to the Myasthenia Gravis Foundation of America). Data were collected on three key outcomes: the risk of progression from ocular myasthenia to generalized myasthenia gravis, improvement in ocular symptoms (such as diplopia or ptosis), and the frequency of treatment-related adverse effects. In the original review, only two RCTs relevant to the treatment of ocular myasthenia were identified. However, only one of these studies reported results aligned with the pre-specified outcome measures of this review. This study included just three participants and was of limited methodological quality. No new RCTs were identified in the searches conducted for this update or previous updates. In the absence of robust RCT data, the review instead summarized findings from available observational studies. The authors concluded that the existing randomized controlled trial data are insufficient to draw definitive conclusions regarding the efficacy of any specific treatment for ocular myasthenia. However, data from several observational studies of reasonable quality suggest that corticosteroids and azathioprine may be effective in reducing the risk of progression from ocular myasthenia to generalized myasthenia gravis.
